title: DDN Goes All In on Software for Exascaler - HPCwire
html:
DDN built its reputation on building and selling super-fast Lustre storage appliances to HPC organizations for gathering data from instruments and running modeling and simulation workloads. Going forward, its fortunes will be tied to developing and selling software-defined storage that enables super-fast storage for HPC and AI users.

That’s the conclusion from DDN’s big announcement at SC26: It’s pivoting away from selling EXAscaler, its Lustre-based storage offering, on hardware. Instead, it’s going to focus on selling EXAscaler as software with the launch of EXAscaler 7 in 2027.

The days of hardware-based EXAscaler devices are numbered

DDN says customers still will be able to buy pre-configured storage appliances from partners. But the days of DDN as a hardware company effectively are over.

“Initially we were deploying full systems,” DDN CEO Alex Bouzari told HPCwire during an interview at SC26. “The technology was all software, but our customers were asking us to deploy a system because they didn’t want to deal with the hardware part of it. So we’re like, okay, fine, we will deploy a system for you.

“Increasingly, as we got very, very successful in AI, as we started landing the large new clouds as customers, the AI natives as customers, well, they each had their own infrastructure. And we said, well, wait a minute. Why can’t we apply the same thing to high-performance computing?”

Today’s AI customers demand more flexibility. They want storage to work across an array of different media. That’s not a problem for DDN, which has been selling its storage as a service in the clouds for a while and has had to adapt to a variety of different storage media. However, the vagaries of today’s storage hardware business are not something that Bouzari wants to bet his business on.

“This is not the old world of HPC, where you knew exactly what the availability was going to be,” he said. “You don’t know today. You don’t know. The cost of SSDs has gone up by a factor of 10.”

The world of AI today requires flexibility in part because of the hardware shortages and the costs, Bouzari continued.

“People who are deploying HPC workloads are relying on a variety of partners,” he said. “GPUs aren’t available, so now I’m going to move to another supplier. Oh, I cannot get allocation for high bandwidth memory from these guys, so now I’m going to use something else.

“So the flexibility in the underlying hardware, I believe, requires an architectural approach for the data engine that is software-defined,” he continued. “That’s why we spend a significant amount of time in taking EXA and making it software-defined, so that it can then be deployed into any data center and can leverage the existing infrastructure that is in place, but also gives people the flexibility you need.”

The AI boom has supercharged DDN’s fortunes, in part because it’s a preferred storage partner for Nvidia. The company has forged a close partnership with the GPU giant, and that has paid off in droves for Bouzari and company, who have not only sold many exabytes of storage to Nvidia, but also to the hyperscaler and neoclouds building AI factories.

DDN has already built flexibility into EXAscaler. It’s already able to run atop a variety of different media types and sizes. Going forward, it will have no trouble being able to run on just about anything, Bouzari said. It will basically have no opinion whatsoever about the hardware.

“It’s completely irrelevant,” Bouzari said of the underlying hardware. “It’s whatever SSD, whatever hard drive. Because, look, I mean, it’s not like there’s 5,000 different types of SSDs and hard drives out there. There’s a small number of OEM providers of servers. There’s a small number of providers of memory and SSDs and drives. And so you have to support the permutations that are associated with that. And those permutations are not infinite. It’s a relatively small number of players that you have to satisfy.”

Being a hardware company is tough these days, whether its servers or storage. Bouzari said there are about 10 companies in the world–Dell, Lenovo, Supermicro, HPE, Nvidia, and the hyperscalers, and Nvidia–that have the skill and heft to build their own hardware, and he doesn’t see that changing over the next three to five years.

“The scale of those companies, it’s north of $100 billion,” he said. “I really don’t see how a customer could trust a company that says, no, don’t worry. I will take care of the hardware for you.”

DDN co-founder and CEO Alex Bouzari

The hardware supply chain crisis has definitely thrown a wrench into many AI and HPC deployment and expansion plans. But Bouzari said he still would have exited DDN from the hardware business even if the price of NVMe and DDR had not gone up by 10x.

“Increasingly in the world of AI, we’re seeing customers requiring a variety of platforms,” he said. “Flexibility I think is the name of the game. And I believe that it’s increasingly the data engine is determining whether your investment in the AI infrastructure is going to be profitable, whatever profitable means for you.”

DDN’s other major project, Infinia, has been software-defined from day one. Infinia is an S3-compatible object store that is geared toward addressing AI needs, particularly AI inference, whereas EXAscaler is heavily used in traditional HPC sectors as well as AI model training, which demands high-performance I/O.

DDN says it’s working on enhancements to EXAScaler in several areas, including multi-tenancy, performance, and data protection. It’s aiming to deliver these new capabilities with version 7 in the first half of 2027.
